lead: Saturday brings two readings about authority. Paul tells the Christians of Rome that governing authority comes from God and that good citizens obey it in conscience. In John, the temple police return without their prisoner, saying, “Never has anyone spoken like this!”, and the leaders argue among themselves. Read together, they set human authority in its place. It has real dignity, it answers to God, and it must itself listen before it judges, as Nicodemus reminds his colleagues.

set: Paul writes around AD 57 to a Church in the capital of the Empire, under the emperor Nero, before the persecution of AD 64. Some years earlier, Jews had been expelled from Rome under Claudius, Aquila and Priscilla among them (Acts 18:2). Many scholars think that Paul wants these Christians to live quietly and to give no reason for further trouble. Some also connect v. 7 with public anger over taxes at about this time.

This passage does not stand alone. Just before it Paul says “Do not repay anyone evil for evil” (12:17), and straight after it he says “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (13:8). It is part of what the life of love looks like in public.
str: vv. 1–2: the principle: authority comes from God.
vv. 3–4: the purpose: to reward good and to punish wrong.
v. 5: the motive: not only fear, but conscience.
vv. 6–7: the practical result: taxes, respect, honour.
kw: Literally to place oneself under, within an order. It is not the same as blind obedience. Paul uses it of keeping one’s place in an order God has given.
The right to act. In the Gospels Jesus has this authority from the Father, and he tells Pilate that Pilate’s authority was “given you from above” (John 19:11).
The word in v. 6, from which “liturgy” comes. Paul calls even the authorities who collect taxes ministers in God’s service, a striking way to set them under God.
vv: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities;
Paul speaks of “every person”, not only Christians. He rejects the idea that being in Christ puts believers above the law of the land.
for it is God’s servant for your good.

The authority is a servant, and its purpose is the common good. This sets a measure by which every government can be judged. The next phrase, about the sword, describes the Rome of Paul’s day. The Church today teaches that the death penalty is inadmissible (CCC 2267).
Therefore one must be subject, not only because of wrath but also because of conscience.
Conscience is the deciding word. A person who obeys from conscience is able also to refuse when an order is evil, which is what Peter and the apostles did (Acts 5:29).
ch: The Catechism quotes this passage when it teaches that authority is required by the moral order and comes from God (CCC 1897–1904, esp. 1899). It also draws from v. 7 the duty of citizens to pay taxes and to share in public life (CCC 2238–2240). And it adds the other side: a citizen is obliged in conscience not to follow orders contrary to the moral order, for “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (Acts 5:29; CCC 2242). St Clement of Rome, in a time of danger, prayed for rulers that God would give them health and peace (1 Clement 61).

r.h: Never has anyone spoken like this
set: The police were sent to arrest Jesus during the festival (7:32), and he has just spoken of living water (7:37–39). They now return to the chief priests and Pharisees with empty hands. The scene shows division among those in authority. Nicodemus, who came to Jesus by night (3:1–2), speaks up for a fair hearing here, and he will bring myrrh and aloes for Jesus’ burial (19:39).

Verse 53 begins the story of the woman taken in adultery (7:53–8:11), which the earliest manuscripts of John do not have. The Church receives the story as inspired Scripture, and the NRSV prints it in brackets.
str: vv. 45–46: the police return and explain.
vv. 50–51: Nicodemus appeals to the law.
kw: Temple attendants who worked under the chief priests. These men had authority to arrest, yet a few words left them unable to do it.
To lead astray. The same charge was heard in the crowd earlier (7:12). The irony is that the men sent to arrest him are accused of being fooled.
In v. 51, literally, “unless it first hears from him”. The law requires a hearing (see Deuteronomy 1:16–17). Those who will not listen cannot judge.
vv: Never has anyone spoken like this!
The police are not theologians and they offer no argument. They just report what they heard. The words of Jesus have done what weapons could not.
“Our law does not judge people without first giving them a hearing to find out what they are doing, does it?”

Nicodemus says “our law”. He speaks as a loyal Pharisee and uses the law to defend Jesus. He is not yet openly a disciple, but he has taken one brave step. That he is one of them shows that no group here can be judged all together.
Surely you are not also from Galilee, are you?

An insult, not an answer. The claim that no prophet comes from Galilee is what these speakers say in anger. Yet 2 Kings 14:25 says that Jonah came from Gath-hepher, a town in Galilee, and an early papyrus of John here reads “the prophet”, which would mean the one foretold by Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15).
ch: The Catechism draws from this passage the honest picture of the leaders of that time. Among the religious authorities of Jerusalem, the Pharisee Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were secret disciples of Jesus, and there was long-standing dissension about him (CCC 595). That is why the Church refuses to lay the responsibility for his death on the Jews as a people (CCC 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4). These harsh words about the crowd come from a few men in a moment of anger and are not the voice of Israel.

qa: Does Romans 13 mean that Christians must obey any government, whatever it does?

No. Paul describes authority as “God’s servant for your good” (13:4). Its right to be obeyed depends on that purpose. When a command goes against God’s law, the Christian must follow God first (Acts 5:29; CCC 2242). Revelation 13 shows the other face of an empire that demands what belongs only to God.
study: How do I speak of those who govern us? Do I pray for them, as well as criticize them?
Am I like Nicodemus, ready to ask for a fair hearing when others have already decided against someone?
